summary: Try settings systematically, and see why random often beats a grid.
headline: Random search wastes fewer trials
overview: Settings you choose before training, like the penalty strength, are hyperparameters. Trying every combination on a grid sounds thorough.
If only one setting really matters, a 3 by 3 grid tries just 3 values of it. Nine random trials try nine.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Make the second setting useless. Now the grid repeats the same few values of the one that matters, and random search tends to win.

check.question: Only one of your two settings really matters. Why can random search beat a grid?
options: It tries more distinct values of the setting that matters
Grids cannot be used with cross-validation

realLife: Whatever you search with, score each trial with cross-validation, then confirm once on data you never touched.
data: A toy score surface with a narrow good region in the first setting. Grid and random each get the same number of trials. The averages are over 300 repeated random draws, with the grid fixed.
maths: trials: grid uses (values per setting)^(settings), which grows exponentially
Bergstra and Bengio found most datasets depend on only a few settings, and which few differs by dataset.
Their random search matched or beat grid-plus-manual tuning on five of seven datasets, so it is not a guaranteed win.
code:
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
from scipy.stats import loguniform
search = RandomizedSearchCV(model, {'C': loguniform(1e-3, 1e3)}, n_iter=20, cv=5).fit(X, y)
